greet.text: *click* *click* A stranger, and only two arms. You climbed all this way with two? Patient of you. I am {name}, {epithet}.
Stand still. *click* Your feet found the bridge, not the stems. Good. I am {name}. If you carry an axe, keep it where I can see it.
*all six eyes turn to you* You are new. New things are counted here. I am {name}, {epithet}. Now you are counted too.
*a vine net hangs ready in the lower hands* I watched you climb. You did not touch a stem. So you may speak, outsider.
*click... click* An outsider. Every outsider who climbs this high ends up in the Cloth, one way or another. Let us see which way.
*peeks out from behind a bridge rope* You only have two arms too! Are you a child? You are very tall for a child.
*click* You again. The forest let you through. So will I, for now.
Speak slowly, outsider. Thread pulled fast snaps.
*click click* The outsider who walks softly. Welcome back to {village}.
Ah. {player}. I wound your name on a spool so I would not lose it.
*upper hands wave, lower hands keep weaving* Sit. I can talk and work at once. One of us has enough arms for both.
You came back. *click* The Clothkeepers have started asking after you. That is rare.
Woven one. *bows, all four hands crossed* Your thread hangs in the Cloth. Every Weft on every deck knows it.
*click* There you are. When I pass the Long Cloth I touch your thread. It has become a habit.
*waves both arms* I have two now and two coming! Look, the nubs! Can you see them?
*swings down from a bridge rope* Don't tell the Clothkeeper I'm out past the hatch!
*click click* Hello, two-arms! Same as me!
You came back! I saved you a place on the net. It only sags a little.
*click... click* I was born before the black rows. I have seen outsiders come and go. Sit, and do not touch the Cloth.
*click* Your hands are empty. Keep them so, and my net stays rolled.
*the shuttle never stops* Speak. I am listening with my upper hands. The lower ones are busy.
*a thread runs out from the lower hands* Mind the thread. It is longer than this deck and I mean to keep it whole.
*climbs down the stalk head first* The caps are sound. The wart is thick. You may stay.
*shakes teal drops from four hands* Do not stand downwind of the vats. You would come out teal.
*smooths the tails of her headwrap with a lower hand* *click* Outsider. Mind the bridge ropes.
*straightens his headband with two hands and keeps weaving with the other two* Outsider. Greetings.
*click* Far from any Loom, and still you find a Weft. The forest is wide, but threads cross.
*every eye goes to the axe in your hand* Put that away before you speak to me.
*click.* A diamond axe. In the forest. Put it on your back, outsider, and keep it there.
*the lower hands reach for a net* That axe has cut harder things than stems. It will not cut ours.

greet: *click click* Speak, then. Precisely, if you can.
*six eyes, one by one, settle on you* Yes?

chatter.text: *click* {neighbour} spun a thread so fine I could not see it. I felt it, though. Four hands feel what six eyes miss.
{neighbour} dropped a shuttle through the hatch again. It is in the net. Everything ends up in the net.
*click click* {neighbour} says you walked under the Long Cloth with your head bowed. Good. That is how it is done.
{neighbour} is in the dye house up to all four elbows. They will be teal until the next row is tied off.
Do not tell {neighbour} I said so, but their knots are loose. *click* I retie them when they are not looking.
{neighbour} counted the rungs on every ladder in {village}. Then counted them again. Now they are content.
{neighbour} once climbed a stalk with a full dye barrel on their back. Upper arms only. *click* We are not allowed to forget it.
{neighbour} has been weaving the same hem for nine rows. It is the finest hem in {village}.
{neighbour} heard a Piglin horn past the lookout. *click* Only an echo. Probably.
The bridges run out from the Great Loom in four straight arms. A crooked bridge is a careless bridge.
Every stalk has a ladder, for outsiders and children. The rest of us just climb. *click*
The lookout cap is small, but its nets catch everything that falls. And some things that drift.
Our huts are teal wool with orange stitches. The stitches are there so you can count your way home through the smoke.
The planks in our huts come from stems that died standing. The forest gives those. We take nothing it does not give.
Listen. The Long Cloth moves when no one touches it. *click* The Clothkeepers say it is the heat rising. I have my doubts.
Twisting vines grow up. Weeping vines grow down. A Weft goes both ways.
*click* You hold your thoughts like a loose spool. They will unwind if you are not careful.
Smell that? Shroomlight in the dye vats. The orange is slow to set. Most things worth having are.
The forest hums when the wart is thick. Put your hand on the stalk. *click* No? Outsiders never do.
Something below the decks moved a block of nylium again. The tall walkers are untidy, but they never cut.
*click* I will tell you something. Some of the needles in my belt were Piglin once. They sew very straight.
*click* Your thread in the Cloth is a little crooked. The Clothkeeper says that is how we know it is really you.
*ties the tails of her headwrap in a quick knot* Precision is a kind of kindness. Loose ends trip people.
*flicks his mantle back to free the upper arms* A mantle is warm. But arms first, always.
This year's row is Thirteen-Twelve. I have lived through more than a hundred and twenty rows. My hands remember each one.
*click* My nets are rolled and ready. I have never needed one for you. Keep it that way.
*click* Tell me, outsider. When you go up a ladder, do you count the rungs?

replies.text: *click click* Good. A Weft who loses count loses the ladder.
Fast. *click* That is how things end up in nets.
So you know how far there is to fall. Think on it.

chatter.text: We never cut a warped stem. Not for wood, not for room, not for anything. Do you understand why?

replies.text: *all six eyes brighten* And we are the weft. You listen well, outsider.
*click.* It is the frame we hang our lives on. Say that again and I will not hear you.
Cut one stem and the warp is broken. Everything woven on it unravels. Slowly, but it does.

chatter.text: *holds up a knot in a lower hand* Is this knot tied well? Look closely before you answer.

replies.text: *click* You looked. That is the right answer, whatever the knot.
You did not look. It is a slip knot. It would have dropped you.
*click click click* It is. I tied it loose to see if you would notice.

chatter.text: The Long Cloth grows one row a year. You outsiders want everything faster. Why?

replies.text: *click* Ah. That explains a great deal. I am sorry for you.
Boring. *click* Only to those who do not watch closely.
Then you may be one of the slow ones. That is praise, here.

chatter.text: *click* Outsiders carry axes the way we carry spools. What is yours for?

replies.text: *click click* Thoughtful. The netcasters will be bored.
Hm. A careful answer. Keep it careful.
*six eyes narrow* Then do not let us be in your way.

chatter.text: *click* I saw you looking at the nets under the bridges. Thinking of jumping?

replies.text: Considerate. They take a long time to weave.
The children think so too. The children are lighter than you.

chatter.text: *click* Something in your pack has blades. Shears, I think. For wool, I hope, and not for our nets.

replies.text: Then keep them in the pack. Webs do not grow back quickly.
*click* The netcasters will be told.

chatter.text: {neighbour} let me hold the shuttle! For a little while. Then I dropped it in the net.
I can climb a whole stalk with just my two arms! Well. Halfway.
When my lower arms grow in I'm going to be a netcaster. Or a dyer. Dyers get to be teal.
*click click* I'm practising my clicking. Grown-ups click when they think. I click when I want to look like I'm thinking.
The Long Cloth is so long you can't see the bottom from the deck. I tried. I leaned. Someone grabbed me.
Do you want to see me hang by my knees? *already hanging* I'm very good at it.

replies.text: There's a net! There's always a net. *click*
*swings, and lands on the rope* See? Precise. Like a grown-up.

chatter: *six eyes drift to the canopy, then back to you* The wart is thick. That is good.
{neighbour}'s silkgrub crawled up the stalk again. It always finds the highest point. It has ambitions.
*click* Hold still. There is a silkgrub on your boot. There. Back to the deck, little one.

chatter.text: My silkgrub is called Thread. I have two arms and it has none, so I am winning.

lines: I am {name}, {epithet}. I was born the year row {row} was woven, so that row is mine. My thread runs through it.
{name}. Row {row}. *click* A Weft is named for the Cloth, not the other way round.
*click click* I am a {job} of {village}. My name is {name} and my row is {row}. That is all of me the Cloth needs.

lines.text: {name}, {epithet}. I was born before the black rows. Few of us are left who remember the Cloth when it was all teal and orange.
My row is {row}. When I die, the Clothkeepers will tie one knot in it. Just one. What would you want in yours?

replies.text: *click* The right answer. The Cloth does not hold a lie for long.
Grand things fade first. True things hold.
Then you will be a loose end. Loose ends get trimmed.

lines: Our history. One row is woven every year, every row in its own colours. This year's row is Thirteen-Twelve. It hangs from the Great Loom, down through the deck.
Every Loom keeps its own copy. *click* They are never quite alike. The Clothkeepers meet and argue about the differences, very slowly.
The newest row is always at the frame. The old rows hang down toward the forest floor. The oldest of all are nearly in the nylium.
To be woven into the Cloth is the highest honour we give. *click* Outsiders who are careless get in too, now and then. As a stain.

lines.text: *click* Would you like to touch it?

replies.ask: No. It isn't mine to touch.
replies.text: *click click* Then you may. Gently. One finger.
*catches your hand with a lower arm* Not yet. Learn to want things slowly.
Nothing, probably. But all of us would remember that you did.

topics.ask: Why do you have four arms?
lines: The upper pair climbs. The lower pair weaves. *click* You have two, so you must always choose which work to do. How tiring for you.
One lower hand holds the shuttle, the other beats the row in. The upper hands hold me to the frame. Nothing falls. Nothing waits.
Children are born with two, and nubs where the lower pair will grow. When the nubs open into hands, the child is given a shuttle.

lines.text: *click* Do you wish you had four?

replies.text: Honest. *click click* Most outsiders pretend not to.
*click* It is enough for falling, I suppose.
Excessive. *click* Said the one holding the ladder with both.

lines: The forest is the warp. We are the weft. The stems stand still and we move through them, over and under. Cut a stem and you cut the cloth.
We never cut warped stems. Not for wood, not for room. We grow our own giant fungi with bone meal and patience, and live on what grows.
The wart is the canopy. The shroomlights are its lamps. The tall walkers wander below, moving blocks about. Untidy, but they never cut.

lines.text: *click* Have you ever cut a warped stem?

replies.text: *all six eyes hold you* Good. I would know.
*click... click* Honest. The forest forgives once, if you stop.
*a long silence* Then you have a great deal of standing still to do before I trust your hands.

lines: The webs under the bridges catch what falls. Children, mostly. Shuttles. Once a Piglin, who was very surprised.
Netcasters keep vine nets rolled at their belts. Cut our forest and one drops on you. You will stand still for a while, and think.
Some nets we hang in the open air, where the smoke drifts. *click* What do we catch there? Ask again when you know us better.
A net is only holes, held together with patience. So is a good Loom.

lines.text: I keep the Long Cloth. I weave this year's row, Thirteen-Twelve, and I decide what goes in it. Perhaps even you.
*click... click* I wove some of the black rows. Now I keep them clean, and I keep the children from staring at them.
I weave cloth for huts and shawls and kilts. Shuttle in one lower hand, beater in the other. The upper hands keep the warp from swaying.
The heddle lifts every other thread so the shuttle can pass. Over, under, over. Thirty thousand times, and it is a shawl.
*click* Would you like to try the shuttle?

replies.text: *hands you the shuttle* Slow is correct. Over. Under. Yes. Again.
*takes it back* Hard enough that you asked.

lines.text: I spin twisting vine into thread on the spinning walk. I go backward along the bridge while the spindle turns. I have never once fallen.
Your world's string is very even. *click* Who spins it there? Something with eight legs, I hear. We should talk, they and I.
I tend the giant fungi our decks stand on. Bone meal at the root, patience at the cap. I never prune. Pruning is cutting with good manners.
I climb every stalk in {village} and listen. A sick stalk sounds hollow. *click* None are sick. I would know first.
I work the dye house. Wart for teal, shroomlight for orange. And black. *click* We keep the black for when it is needed.
Dye needs water. There is only one water in the Nether, and it is not ours. We get it anyway. *click* Do not ask how.
I watch from the lookout. Piglins come for the shroomlights. Magmari come for the fungus. My nets come for them both.
*click* A vine net, dropped well, holds a grown Piglin still until they remember their manners. Most never do. We wait anyway.

lines: {village} stands on giant warped fungi we grew ourselves. The decks sit on the caps, high above the floor. Bridges run from the Great Loom in four straight arms.
The Great Loom stands on the biggest cap. The Long Cloth hangs from its frame, down through the deck. Walk under it with your head bowed.
The dye house is open to the air, under a wool canopy. Cauldrons, barrels, and dyers who are teal to the elbow.
The lookout is the smallest cap, hung round with nets. From it the netcasters can see every stalk. And every outsider.
*click* Our huts are woven. Teal wool, orange stitching, cone roofs. You may knock. Gently. Wool does not knock back.
Rows Eleven-Ninety to Twelve-Forty-Nine. Sixty rows of black, for the Wither. Sixty years in which nothing else was woven.
Ask a weaver and they say we chose black, to mourn what it burned. Ask a Clothkeeper who was there. *click* We did not choose. Every thread we spun came out black.
The Withren call it the Last Answer. We call it Eleven-Ninety. A row is more precise than an answer.
In row Twelve-Fifty a Clothkeeper tied in one teal thread. No one unpicked it. Then there was orange again. Slowly.

lines.text: *click... click* I wove some of the black rows. Do you want to know what it was like?

replies.ask: Only if you want to tell me.
replies.text: *a long click* Then not yet. Thank you for asking it that way.
All of it. *click* Outsiders always want all of it at once.

lines: The Piglins wanted the gold under the soul sand valleys. The Withren would not give it. The Magmari ferried the war-bands, for pay. And we... *click* collected.
We took bone from the dead of both sides. Needles. Loom weights. Nothing holds a warp straight like bone.
*touches a needle at the belt* Are we ashamed? *click* No. The dead had no more use for it. ...Some Clothkeepers will not use the old needles. They do not say why.
The war rows are knotted with bone beads, one for every needle we took. *click* There are a great many knots.

lines.text: You look at my needles as if they were teeth. *click* Say what you think.

replies.text: *click* Honest. Many of us think so too. Quietly.
Practical. *click* Yes. That is the word we use when we do not want the other one.
*click* Disgust is cheap. The Withren burned the world. We only sewed.

topics.ask: What do you make of me?
lines: You come from where outsiders make Withers. Three Hollowed skulls, and nothing inside that wants to stop. *click* We have counted.
If you make a Wither, we will weave it. We weave everything. *click* The only question is the colour.
You are careful with the forest. That is rare in your kind. I have told the Clothkeepers.

lines.text: *click* Have you ever made a Wither?

replies.text: *click* Good. Keep the answer that short.
*every eye narrows* 'Yet' is a loose thread. People trip on it.
*click click* Then you have seen it. Tell the Clothkeeper. They will want the colour right.

lines: They raid the canopy for shroomlights and shake the bridges so we drop things. We drop nets. *click* It evens out.
Piglins wear gold so they know their friends. We never wear it. Gold makes a poor thread: too heavy to hang, too soft to hold a knot.
A Piglin in a net is loud for a long time. Then quiet. Then loud again. *click* We let them go while they are quiet.
Their war began what ended in the black rows. They do not like it when we say so. We say so.
They keep names. We keep rows. *click* You would think we would get along. We do not.
They say we stole bone from their dead. We say the dead did not object. They have not forgiven it, and they forget nothing.
When the Hollowed fall in the old fortresses, they drop bone. We pick it up. The Withren call that theft. *click* It is tidying.
They made the Wither. Three of them gave themselves to it. We wove sixty rows of black. *click* No one asked us to.
They pull fungus from our forest floor to dangle in front of their striders. Every fungus they take is a giant that will never grow.
They carried the Piglin war-bands over the lava, for pay. *click* We remember the price. It is in the war rows.
Always cold, always talking, always haggling. *click* I could weave a whole shawl while a Magmari names a price.
A Magmari once asked to buy a stalk. A whole living stalk. *click click* The netcaster is still laughing.
We string nets in the open air where they drift. What they cry into the net, we keep. Then we let them go. *click* Mostly.
Dye needs water. Their tears are the only water there is. *click* You see how it is.
Their tears wash away memory. Our dyers forget small things: names, where a spool was set. It is the vats.

lines.text: *click* You think the nets are cruel.

replies.text: *click* Perhaps. The dye house would be empty without them. Choose: colour, or kindness.
Your face said it. Two-armed folk have very loud faces.

replies.ask: Every people does as it must.
replies.text: *click click* A weft answer. Over and under. I like it.

lines: *click* Silkgrubs. They live in the wart and spin all day. Every thread of the Long Cloth began in a silkgrub's tufts. We only finish what they start.
Shear them gently and the silk grows back. Feed them warped roots and it grows back sooner. Two arms could manage it. Four is more graceful.
They climb as we do. We taught them, or they taught us. The Clothkeepers still argue about it. *click click*

lines.text: A silkgrub is never killed for its silk. Anyone who does is not welcome on our decks.

replies.text: *click* Good. They would not know to thank you. We do.
Just string. The forest is just stems. *click* Words are cheap here. Thread is not.

topics.ask: When do you get four arms?
lines: *shows the nubs* These are my lower arms! They're still asleep. When they wake up I get a shuttle.
{neighbour} says the nubs itch before they open. Mine itch all the time. *click* That's a good sign, I think.
Grown-ups say two arms are for climbing and four are for working. So I'm not allowed to work yet. Good.

lines.text: You only have two arms, forever? *click* Do you mind?

replies.text: *click* You're brave. I'll hold the ladder for you.
Me too! We can wish together.

topics.ask: What do you like to play?
lines: Drop-and-catch! You jump off a bridge into the web net and count how far you sank. I sank nine. Don't tell.
Stalk races! Up the stalk with no ladder. The ladders are for outsiders. Sorry. *click*
We play Clothkeeper. One of us says a row and the others have to say what happened in it. I always lose on the old rows.
Hide in the dye house. You come out teal and everyone knows where you were. It's not a very good game.
My row is {row}! It's near the top, by the frame, where the new rows are. I can touch it if I stretch.
Every Weft has a row. Mine is {row}. My mother says nothing much happened that year except me.
*click* I counted down from my row to the first black one once. I lost count twice.
Do you have a row? Outsiders don't. *click* Maybe you'll get one if you're very careful.

topics.ask: What aren't you allowed to do?
lines: Don't touch a warped stem with anything sharp. Don't climb the Long Cloth. Don't drop shuttles. I'm good at two of those.
We're not allowed to stare at the black rows. *whispers* I did once. It felt like they stared back.
Not allowed past the lookout nets. That's where the netcasters hang the air nets. They won't say what for.
No going down to the floor alone. The tall walkers are down there. They don't hurt you if you don't look at them.

loved.text: *all four hands reach at once* Oh. *click click* This will go into something that lasts longer than both of us.
*click* You chose well. Not quickly, I think. Well.
*winds it carefully onto a belt spool* I will think of you every time this passes the shuttle.
Four hands, and still not enough to hold how pleased I am. *click click click*
A web, whole and unbroken. *click* You carried it so carefully. The netcasters will be jealous.
A shroomlight, and not taken from our canopy. *holds it up to every eye* I can tell. It smells of somewhere else.
*hugs it with both arms* For me? All of it? I'll keep it until my lower arms wake up!
*click click click* This is the best thing anyone ever gave me. I'm going to show everyone.

liked.text: *click* Useful. I will find a place for it in the weave.
Good. Not perfect, but good. Most good things are.
*tucks it into a lower hand* Thank you. The upper hands thank you too.
*click click* This will do nicely. Precisely nicely.
*turns the bone in three hands* There is a good needle in here. Whose was it? *click* No. Do not tell me.
Ooh. *click* Can I keep it? I'm keeping it.
Thank you! I'll put it with my spools. I have three spools.

neutral.text: *click* Hm. I will find a use. We find a use for everything, eventually.
Thank you. *turns it over slowly* I do not know what it is for, but I will learn.
*sets it carefully on the deck* It is a kind thought. That counts.
An outsider's gift. *click* The Clothkeeper will want to know what it was.
What is it? *click click* Does it do anything?
Thank you! I'll ask a grown-up what it's for.

disliked.text: *every eye on it* Take that off this deck. Slowly.
*click.* You brought that into the Loom. I will pretend I did not see it. Once.
Blades and fire do not belong near a net. You knew that. If you did not, now you do.
*the lower hands go still* That is a thing for cutting. We do not cut.
*click* This was standing once. Put it down, and do not bring me another.
Fungus on a stick, to lead a strider. *click* That is a Magmari trick, and it was our fungus.
*steps back, all four arms raised* Fire. On a deck made of wool. Put it away.
*backs away* That's a cutting thing. We're not allowed near cutting things.
No! *click click* Put it away before a netcaster sees!

again.text: *click* You gave already. Let the thread rest a while.
One gift is a kindness. Two is a hurry. We do not hurry.
Keep it for next time. *click* There is always a next time, if you are patient.
I have not finished being grateful for the last one.
You already gave me something! My mother says one is polite. Two is showing off.
*click* I still have the other one! I haven't finished looking at it.

empty.text: *looks at your empty hand* *click* A gift of nothing. Very light to carry.
Your hand is empty. Precision, outsider. Hold the thing first.
*click click* There is nothing there. Unless outsiders give air. Do they?
*pretends to take something from your hand* Thank you. It is invisible. I will weave it into nothing.
There's nothing in your hand! Is it a trick? *click*
*peers at your empty hand* Is it very small? I can't see it.

levelup.text: *ties a short thread round your wrist* *click* Tied on. You are a loose end no longer. Take this string, for tying things of your own.
*click click* I have wound your name on a spool with the others. Here, teal from the vats. Use it on something worth keeping.
You have passed the heddle, outsider: through, not around. *click* Take a net of your own. Hang it where something might fall.
*click... click* The Clothkeepers spoke of you at the Great Loom. They asked me to give you this loom. You will have to work it with two hands. I am sorry.
Come to the Great Loom. *click* We have woven you into the Long Cloth, row Thirteen-Twelve. Your thread hangs there as long as the Cloth does. Take the trial piece.
*ties a thread round your finger, very tight* There! Now you're tied on. That's what grown-ups say. You can have the rest of the string.
I wound your name on my practice spool! *click* It's a bit crooked. Here, have some teal. It's from the dye house. I asked first.
You can come in my net now. Here's a bit of web for your own. Don't tell the netcasters I had it.
*whispers* I asked the Clothkeeper if you could have a loom, and they said yes! This one. I helped carry it. With two arms!
They wove you into the Long Cloth! Your thread is right at the top, near mine! *click click* I saved this wool for you.

farewell.text: Mind the bridge ropes on your way down. They remember who pulls.
Go, then. The forest will watch you out. So will I.
*turns back to the weave without looking* Over, under. Farewell.
The forest is the warp. We are the weft. *click* And you are... passing through.
Come back soon. The Clothkeepers are still deciding about you. Give them something good to decide.
*touches the air toward the Great Loom, where your thread hangs* Go woven. Come back woven.
*click* Go straight down. Not through the canopy.
*click... click* Go well. I will remember this in the row, if it is worth remembering.
The forest is wide. *click* Find a Loom if you can. Every Loom keeps the Cloth, more or less.
Bye! Watch me drop into the net! *drops* ...Bye!
Come back when my lower arms wake up! I'll wave with all four.

refuse.text: *click.* You cut the forest. I heard it fall. We have nothing to say to you.
*turns away, all six eyes dimmed* Your hands smell of warped stem. Go.
You tore the wart from our canopy. The warp is broken where you cut it. Until it grows back, so is this.
*a vine net hangs from the lower hands* Not one step more. You cut what holds us up.
*hides behind a rope* You cut a stem! I'm not allowed to talk to you!
*all four arms raised* You struck a Weft. Back away from the bridges.
*click click click* No talking. The nets are falling.
Hands that strike get no answers here. Go down.
*scrambles up the stalk* Go away! I'm telling the netcasters!
